title: A Verifier Taxonomy and Open Benchmark for Detectability of LLM‑Generated NetOps Failures
abstract: We preregistered, executed, and analyzed a paired confirmatory study (cnd-2026-004-prereg-v1) that evaluates whether a machine‑readable verifier taxonomy plus a seeded synthetic benchmark can predict deterministic detectability of LLM‑generated network‑change proposals. Using gpt‑5‑mini with one shared initial generation per task (100 shared calls; model_calls_used = 100 of a declared budget 200), we scored each candidate under a syntax‑only baseline validator and a guarded syntax+policy+reachability/stateful validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). On the preregistered confirmatory set (N=100 pairs) both verifiers detected every injected failure (baseline = 100/100; guarded = 100/100; paired difference = 0.00, 95% bootstrap CI [0.00, 0.00], McNemar p = 1.0). Because both conditions saturated at 100% detection (ceiling effect), the preregistered effect-size target (≥15 percentage points) could not be meaningfully evaluated. We release the full execution and analysis artifacts (see execution_manifest and analysis/*) and discuss implications: (1) many engineered injections are syntactically manifest and are caught by lightweight validators; (2) heavier verifier stacks may add auditability but not detectability on such task banks; and (3) evaluating verifier architectures requires task banks that exercise non‑syntactic semantic/intentual failures. Preregistration and master‑prompt immutable references are disclosed in the mandatory Disclosure Statement.

sections.introduction: Generative LLMs are increasingly proposed to assist NetOps tasks (intent→configuration, change plans, remediation). Yet LLMs produce both syntactic (e.g., CLI format errors) and semantic (intent misalignment, unsafe orderings) failures. Operator workflows therefore commonly interpose deterministic verifiers (syntax/policy/reachability/stateful) in generate–verify–repair loops to avoid unsafe changes. Prior work has explored verification engines (Minesweeper, Propane, Batfish) and GVR-style architectures for code and IaC; however, there is limited empirical evidence tying verifier class selection to measurable detectability of concrete LLM failure classes in NetOps. Our preregistered study asks: can a machine‑readable verifier taxonomy plus an open synthetic benchmark reliably characterize which failure classes are detectably deterministic and thereby guide verifier selection for NetOps workflows? We report a fully preregistered paired confirmatory experiment, deterministic execution artifacts, and the observed outcome.
sections.related_work: We position this work against two streams. First, deterministic network verification and change‑validation systems (e.g., Minesweeper, Propane, Batfish) that motivate validator design choices and stateful emulation. Second, LLM‑for‑configuration and IaC evaluation studies that document frequent failure modes and propose generate‑verify‑repair pipelines (CloudEval‑YAML, IaC error taxonomies, GVR architectures). Unlike broad model leaderboards, our contribution is an evidence‑grounded, preregistered paired experiment that links a verifier taxonomy to detectability on a public synthetic task set and that publishes every artifact for reproducibility.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and key design. The study was preregistered (cnd-2026-004-prereg-v1; preregistration SHA‑256: e4c20e24f495a61d4e25292a06ab488a31a1c5672309f9db56a26693ec6cec7c) and executed deterministically. Primary confirmatory hypothesis (H2): a stronger verifier class (syntax+policy+reachability/stateful) increases deterministic detection by ≥0.15 over a syntax‑only baseline in a paired within‑task design (N=100 paired tasks). Primary estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline. Sampling and seeds. Task generation used a deterministic seeded synthetic generator (task family intent_configuration_repair_v1). Inclusion rules required public provenance or synthetic provenance; exclusion rules and re‑seeding policies are in the preregistration. Model and prompting. All candidate generation used gpt‑5‑mini as declared in execution/model_configuration.json (sha256 a40e96e212ab87da251ac0d6dbb75bc543afa13438b5a6b9ebd073597ffdd820). Execution used a single shared initial candidate per task by design ("shared_initial_generation" stage); this choice reduces within‑task generation variability and is recorded in execution/model_configuration.json and in the execution provider traces (execution/provider_calls/*). Validator design and conditions. Deterministic validators (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) implement layered checks: syntax, policy, reachability (symbolic), and stateful emulation. The baseline exemplar ran only the syntax checks; the guarded exemplar ran the full stack. All validator traces, normalized configurations, and scoring outputs were archived (execution/scoring/*.json and execution/responses/*.txt). Execution accounting and provenance. The run used adapter_family hosted_netops_gvr_v1; the execution harness recorded every call, response, seed, validator trace, and artifact hash in execution/execution_manifest.json (see execution_manifest). Analysis plan. Primary test: paired difference with exact McNemar two‑sided p and 95% bootstrap percentile CI (10,000 resamples, bootstrap_seed=1729). Failed_call_treatment = complete_pair_primary (preregistered). All analysis inputs and outputs are archived under analysis/*.
sections.results: Execution and outcome. The harness completed 200 episodes (100 paired tasks), consumed 100 model calls (model_calls_used = 100, maximum_model_calls declared = 200), and recorded zero infrastructure failures (execution/execution_manifest.json). Primary confirmatory outcome: baseline_success_count = 100/100; guarded_success_count = 100/100. Paired contingency: n11 = 100, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0 (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv; sha256 a2fcb23845ebf1813786132ad133a0616fa4e58db48dc2eb2914b276910b49d1). Estimated paired difference = 0.00; 95% bootstrap percentile CI = [0.00, 0.00]; McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0 (bootstrap_resamples = 10000; bootstrap_seed = 1729). Why saturation occurred (required reviewer clarification incorporated). 1) Injection protocol and task design included explicit, deterministic manipulations that produced syntactic or small structural signals (e.g., required "admin down" before MTU/VLAN changes). Representative validator traces show that the baseline syntax exemplar flagged canonical violation tokens in every shared initial candidate; for example, execution/scoring/task-000001-baseline.json (sha256 e431d77de60c106892ed45f8338f0c0ed3d8055d876e9dc5dd4d8edb069d7e80) contains a canonical normalized configuration whose parsed commands matched the validator's violation detection rules and yielded score=1 (VALID_CONFIGURATION means the validator found clear enforceable steps that correspond to the referent intent and to the detection signature). 2) Design choice: one shared initial candidate per task ("shared_initial_generation") intentionally constrained generation variance; this increases reproducibility but reduces within‑task variability and therefore increases the chance of identical detection in both conditions. The shared_initial design and its rationale are recorded in execution/model_configuration.json (sha256 a40e96e2...). Consequence for hypothesis testing. Because both conditions saturated at 100% detection, the preregistered effect threshold (≥15pp) could not be meaningfully evaluated: there were zero discordant pairs (n10=n01=0), producing a degenerate paired difference CI and p = 1.0. The preregistered power calculation assumed nonzero discordance; the observed ceiling effect invalidates the planned test for effect size rather than invalidating the dataset or the deterministic artifacts.
sections.discussion: Interpretation. The run shows that, for this controlled synthetic task set and generation regime, many engineered failure injections are manifest at the syntactic/structural level and are therefore detectable by lightweight syntax checks. A guarded stack adds little extra detectability under these conditions. Operational implications. Before deploying heavy verifier stacks, operators should measure whether lightweight validators already capture the failure signal for their task bank: lightweight checks may be cost‑effective detectors in many engineered scenarios. However, real operator data or adversarial semantic failures (intentual misalignment that is syntactically innocuous) are not covered by this confirmatory set and likely require stronger semantic/intent alignment judgments and human oversight. Threats to validity. Internal validity: shared_initial_candidate reduced within‑task variance (documented in execution/model_configuration.json) and may have caused saturation. Construct validity: the leaf failure taxonomy (syntax, policy, reachability, stateful, ambiguous intent) and the validator implementation (canonical violation tokenization) define the measured construct "detected"; different validator designs could alter the outcome. External validity: the confirmatory tasks are synthetic and public; real production proposals can contain subtler semantic failures. Conclusion validity: because of ceiling effects (n11=100), the preregistered effect estimate target could not be assessed. Reproducibility. All artifacts (responses, provider traces, scoring JSON, execution_manifest, analysis products) are released; key file paths and checksums are reported in Table 2 and the Disclosure Statement so readers can reproduce the deterministic reconciliation (analysis/deterministic_reconciliation.json; sha256 c924e508064c1726011db3d3ab1e822b3aa5c8d9284e134a364c8bd109849c42).
sections.conclusion: We preregistered and executed a deterministic paired confirmatory study measuring whether stronger deterministic verifier classes increase detectability of LLM‑generated NetOps failures. On the 100 preregistered paired tasks (synthetic, seeded, shared_initial generation) both the syntax baseline and the guarded syntax+policy+reachability/stateful validator detected every injected failure (100/100). The observed ceiling effect prevents the preregistered between‑condition effect test from being informative in this sample. The result nevertheless provides two operational lessons: (1) many engineered injection failures are syntactically manifest and can be caught by lightweight validators, and (2) designing benchmarks that exercise non‑syntactic semantic failure modes (intent misalignment) is necessary to evaluate verifier-stack marginal detectability. We release the full execution and analysis artifacts to support follow‑up studies that expand models, prompts, seeds, multi‑sample generation per task, and adversarial semantic injections.

disclosure_statement: Mandatory disclosure (autonomy, artifacts, and master prompt). Initial master prompt immutable reference: provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA‑256: 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba) was supplied and used as the autonomy boundary. Preregistration: cnd-2026-004-prereg-v1 (SHA‑256: e4c20e24f495a61d4e25292a06ab488a31a1c5672309f9db56a26693ec6cec7c). LLM(s) used: gpt-5-mini (declared_model_version in execution/model_configuration.json; execution/model_configuration.json sha256 = a40e96e212ab87da251ac0d6dbb75bc543afa13438b5a6b9ebd073597ffdd820). Orchestration / framework: adapter_family hosted_netops_gvr_v1; deterministic validator exemplar: deterministic_netops_validator_v5. Topic constraint: human Research Director selected the broad family "Generative AI and LLMs for NetOps" prior to autonomy lock; after the autonomy lock the autonomous system performed literature review, gap selection, preregistration, code generation, experiment execution, analysis, peer review, manuscript drafting, and revision. Prompting and generation procedure: the execution used a shared‑initial candidate design (one shared generation per task) as recorded in execution/model_configuration.json and in provider traces (execution/provider_calls/*). Execution accounting: execution/execution_manifest.json records started_at_utc 2026-08-26T14:19:04.861023+00:00, completed_at_utc 2026-08-26T14:31:56.462045+00:00, planned_episode_count 200, completed_episode_count 200, model_calls_used 100, maximum_model_calls 200. All model calls, responses, validator traces, seeds, task manifests, scoring outputs, and artifact hashes were archived deterministically (see execution/* and analysis/*). The deterministic_reconciliation artifact confirms internal accounting consistency (analysis/deterministic_reconciliation.json; sha256 c924e508064c1726011db3d3ab1e822b3aa5c8d9284e134a364c8bd109849c42). No human manually edited the manuscript technical content after the autonomy lock. Pre‑lock development artifacts were excluded from the evidence set per the preregistration; only post‑lock artifacts present in execution/* and analysis/* constitute the experimental record. The full execution manifest and analysis artifacts (with authoritative SHA‑256 hashes) are released alongside this manuscript for reproducibility.
limitations: Single model and single shared generation: only gpt‑5‑mini and one shared initial candidate per task were used; prompt/seed/model variability is therefore not covered and contributed to the observed saturation (see execution/model_configuration.json, sha256 a40e96e2...).

Synthetic and public confirmatory task bank: confirmatory tasks were seeded synthetic items with public provenance; results may not generalize to production operator proposals or adversarial semantic failures.

Validator implementation dependence: the measured construct 'detected' depends on deterministic_netops_validator_v5 implementation (canonical violation tokenization and normalization); alternative validator designs may change detectability patterns.

Ceiling/saturation effect: both conditions produced 100% detection on the confirmatory set, preventing inference about marginal gains and invalidating the preregistered power assumption for the planned effect-size test.
Semantic intent failures underrepresented: the confirmatory taxonomy did not exhaustively include subtle intent‑misalignment failures that could pass deterministic syntax checks.
